question: Long before chocolate became a sweet bar, how did people in Mesoamerica commonly enjoy cacao?
note: Cacao drinks have a long history in Mesoamerica, including what is now Mexico. Sweet chocolate bars came much later; the early drinks were quite different from today’s milky hot chocolate.

question: Which fruit gives guacamole its creamy green base?
note: The name comes from Nahuatl words for avocado and sauce. Early versions combined avocado with tomatoes and chillies, crushed together in a stone mortar.

question: Nachos sound like a name for a snack. What does the name actually remember?
choices: The nickname of the man credited with making them
The town where the first tortillas were baked
A word meaning “crunchy” in an Indigenous language
The name of the cheese originally used
note: Ignacio “Nacho” Anaya is credited with creating the dish in the Mexican border town of Piedras Negras. “Nacho’s special” became a food name that travelled far beyond the man who made it.

question: The vanilla in familiar cakes and ice cream originally came from a Mexican plant. What kind of plant produces vanilla pods?
note: Vanilla was cultivated in the Totonac region of Veracruz and Puebla before the Spanish arrived. It was also used to flavour cacao drinks, long before it became familiar in cakes and ice cream.

question: In Mexico, chocolate can turn up in mole, a sauce served with meat. What does that tell you about chocolate?
choices: It can be an ingredient in savoury cooking
It must always be sweetened before use
It can only be used in cold sauces
It replaces every spice in a sauce
note: Some moles combine chocolate with chillies, seeds and other ingredients to make a savoury sauce. Mole is a whole family of sauces, and many versions contain no chocolate.

question: A chilli pepper can make a person’s mouth burn. Which animal can eat it without that same fiery sensation?
note: Birds do not react to the pepper’s capsaicin the way mammals do. They can eat the fruits and spread the seeds—a useful partnership behind an ingredient so familiar in Mexican cooking.

question: The domestic turkeys raised for meals today trace their ancestry to birds domesticated in which place?
note: The modern domestic turkey descends from birds domesticated in Mexico. Some travelled to Europe and later back across the Atlantic, giving a familiar festive meal a surprisingly roundabout history.

question: Caesar salad sounds as though it belongs to ancient Rome. Which city is associated with its creation?
note: The best-known account credits Italian immigrant Caesar Cardini’s restaurant in Tijuana. The exact inventor and circumstances are disputed, but the name is not a tribute to Julius Caesar.

question: Tequila comes from a spiky plant that can look like a cactus. What is the plant actually called?
note: Tequila is made from agave, not from a cactus. The plant-shaped landscape around Tequila is so closely tied to the drink’s history that UNESCO recognises the fields and old distilleries together.

question: A rotating stack of meat in a Mexican taco shop can look familiar to someone who knows shawarma. Which migrants helped create that connection?
note: Lebanese migrants brought a cooking tradition that was adapted into one of Mexico City’s signature street foods. The rotating meat stack remained, while locally seasoned pork and corn tortillas made the dish distinct.

question: If you could look beneath central Mexico City, what earlier city would you find traces of?
choices: An Indigenous capital built before the Spanish conquest
A colonial port abandoned when its harbour dried up
A Spanish mining settlement destroyed by an earthquake
A royal resort built for a visiting French emperor
note: The Spanish built their city over Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital. At nearby Xochimilco, canals and artificial islands preserve another part of the valley’s older landscape.

question: The pyramid at Chichén Itzá is one of Mexico’s most familiar images. Which civilisation built this city?
note: Chichén Itzá was a Maya city, with buildings that also show influences from central Mexico. Mexico’s ancient monuments belong to different peoples and periods, rather than to one single civilisation.

question: Parts of Mexico City are slowly sinking. What human activity is a major cause?
choices: Pumping water from beneath the old lakebed
Mining away salt deposits under the streets
The weight of buildings bending solid bedrock
Deep subway tunnels draining the surface canals
note: Removing groundwater causes the soft ground under the city to compact. The modern capital still lives with the consequences of being built on an ancient lakebed.

question: Yucatán’s cenotes are natural pools that can open into caves. What process made these inviting swimming holes?
choices: An extinct volcanic crater filling with rain
A river cutting off one of its bends
Sea waves enclosing a coastal lagoon
note: Rainwater dissolves limestone and opens underground cavities. Where a cave roof collapses, the water is exposed; cenotes were important water sources for Maya communities.

question: Which insects gather in such numbers in central Mexico’s mountain forests that their weight can bend branches?
note: Monarch butterflies spend the winter clustered in these mountain forests. Their annual migration cycle spans several generations, so the whole round trip is larger than one butterfly’s lifetime.

question: The axolotl, a Mexican salamander often seen as a smiling little creature, has a remarkable ability. What can it do after losing a leg?
choices: Heal the wound but keep a stump
Replace the leg with a smaller fin
Grow a new limb only before adulthood
note: This Mexican salamander can rebuild a functional limb, which makes it valuable to regeneration research. It also keeps external gills into adulthood and normally remains in the water.

question: Why do grey whales travel to the sheltered lagoons of Baja California in winter?
choices: Rest through winter without eating or moving
note: The lagoons of Ojo de Liebre and San Ignacio are important breeding grounds within El Vizcaíno. Mexico’s desert coast is also a nursery for these ocean travellers.

question: Before it became a US state, California was part of which country?
note: California passed from Mexico to the United States under the treaty that ended the Mexican-American War in 1848. The border moved, leaving a Mexican chapter inside what is now familiar American geography.

question: Buried beneath part of Mexico’s Yucatán region is evidence of which event that changed life on Earth?
choices: The asteroid impact linked to the dinosaurs’ mass extinction
A volcanic eruption that began the last ice age
The earthquake that opened the Atlantic Ocean
The crater left by the largest eruption in human history
note: The enormous Chicxulub impact crater dates to about 66 million years ago. The impact and its aftermath helped wipe out the non-avian dinosaurs, connecting a Mexican landscape to a global turning point.

question: Mexico City’s Xochimilco canals run between artificial islands. What was their practical purpose before they became a famous visitor attraction?
note: These human-made farming plots occupy a landscape of canals and lake areas. They are part of a food-growing tradition that UNESCO includes in its account of Mexican cuisine.

question: Day of the Dead can look like a festival of skeletons. What is at the heart of it?
choices: Remembering relatives and loved ones who have died
Marking the beginning of the new year
Welcoming the first rains of spring
note: Families may prepare an ofrenda with photographs and foods associated with the people they remember. Practices vary between communities, bringing personal memories into a shared annual celebration.

question: Why do families traditionally lay trails of marigolds for Día de los Muertos?
choices: To guide loved ones’ spirits home
To show the route of the children’s procession
To mark houses hosting wedding guests
To symbolise the boundary of a private garden
note: In the tradition, the flowers’ colour and scent help the dead find their way to the ofrenda. Photographs and favourite foods make that welcome personal.

question: Mexico City launched a spectacular new Day of the Dead parade in 2016. What helped inspire its format?
choices: A parade staged for a James Bond film
A newly discovered Aztec festival manual
An old painting showing the same annual route
A royal procession preserved from colonial times
note: Spectre opened with a fictional parade filmed in Mexico City, and a real parade followed. The film influenced this particular public event, not the much older Day of the Dead traditions themselves.

question: Under its colourful paper, what traditionally formed the breakable body of a Mexican Christmas piñata?
note: The traditional piñata covered an earthenware pot with bright paper and filled it with treats. The decorated container was meant to be broken so its fruit and sweets could fall to the waiting group.

question: Before Christmas, groups in Mexico go from door to door in Las Posadas. Whose search for shelter are they acting out?
note: The celebrations recall Mary and Joseph’s search for lodging. In Mexico they run from 16 to 24 December, often joining a procession with food and a piñata.

question: Cinco de Mayo is often marketed abroad as Mexico’s Independence Day. What does it actually commemorate?
choices: A Mexican victory over French troops
The end of Spanish colonial rule
The adoption of the current national flag
The signing of a peace treaty with the United States
note: The date remembers the Battle of Puebla in 1862. Mexico’s Independence Day is in September, so the two celebrations recall different struggles.

question: In the nineteenth century, Mexico briefly had an emperor born in Vienna. What was his background?
choices: A Mexican general educated in Austria
A French merchant elected by parliament
note: Maximilian accepted Mexico’s crown with French support and the backing of Mexican conservatives. His story connects Mexican political conflict with the dynastic ambitions of Europe.

question: Mexico’s flag shows an eagle, a cactus and a snake. The emblem points back to the story of what?
choices: The founding of the city beneath Mexico City
The first Spanish landing on the coast
The discovery of Mexico’s largest silver mine
The signing of the independence declaration
note: The emblem draws on the founding legend of Tenochtitlan. Its familiar modern form developed through different historical versions; it is more than a collection of national wildlife.

question: A Mexican game called lotería plays a little like bingo. What do players match on their boards instead of numbers?
note: A caller announces a card and players cover its matching picture. Dried beans can serve as markers, bringing a kitchen staple onto the game board.

question: In Mexico’s Voladores ceremony, four performers circle down through the air on ropes. What are they descending from?
note: A musician remains at the top, playing a flute and small drum. The ceremony is especially associated with Totonac communities and expresses a relationship with the natural and spiritual worlds.

question: Frida Kahlo painted while confined to bed after an accident. What was fitted above the bed to help her see her subject?
note: Her mother had a mirror installed on the four-poster bed. It made her own face available as a subject; the bed and mirror can be seen at the Casa Azul museum.

question: Diego Rivera painted a mural for New York’s Rockefeller Center, but it was later destroyed. What was at the centre of the dispute?
choices: He included a portrait of Lenin and refused to remove it
He used paint that was forbidden inside tall buildings
He painted over a historic mural without permission
He refused to add the building’s name in larger letters
note: Rivera’s patrons objected to the communist leader’s portrait in Man at the Crossroads. The conflict ended with the mural covered and then removed from the wall—a commission that became a clash over who controlled its message.

question: Mexico’s colourful alebrijes can combine wings, horns and body parts from different animals. What are these figures?
choices: Portraits of a single ancient royal family
Scientific models used in biology classes
note: Pedro Linares developed these figures in Mexico City using cartonería, a paper-and-paste craft. In his account, the strange creatures came from a dream during an illness. His family continued the practice.

question: The elegant Mexican skeleton in a fancy hat became an icon. What did the original image behind La Catrina poke fun at?
choices: Doctors who refused to treat the poor
Actors who forgot their lines on stage
note: Printmaker José Guadalupe Posada used skeletons for social satire, including mockery of elites adopting European fashions. The grand hat makes status look ridiculous when its wearer is reduced to bones.

question: Chemicals extracted from a Mexican wild yam helped pave the way for which major medicine?
note: Chemicals from Mexican yams provided material for producing steroid hormones more affordably. Further research in Mexico helped lead to the oral contraceptive pill; the plant was a starting material, not a ready-made medicine.

question: Sor Juana, a seventeenth-century Mexican writer who defended women’s learning, built her intellectual life in which setting?
note: She maintained a study and library in the convent and spoke with scholars from the court and university. Her writing also argued for women’s access to learning.

question: Which everyday English food word travelled through Spanish from Nahuatl, an Indigenous language of Mexico?
note: Tomato comes through Spanish tomate from Nahuatl tomatl. The ingredient’s journey carried its name into other languages, leaving a Mexican linguistic connection on menus around the world.

question: In the Mexican novel Like Water for Chocolate, Tita cannot freely express her feelings. What gives them a magical way out?
choices: The food she cooks affects the people who eat it
The clothes she sews change colour with her mood
The letters she hides begin speaking aloud
The flowers she grows repeat her secrets
note: Laura Esquivel makes cooking carry Tita’s love, grief and desire beyond what she can say openly. A familiar idea—putting feeling into food—becomes literally powerful inside the story.

question: Maya mathematicians developed a way to write “nothing” as part of their number system. Which familiar idea was that?
note: Maya mathematics included zero and supported sophisticated calendar calculations. An apparent absence became something that could be written and used in a numerical system.

question: A brilliant red used in dyes and pigments has long been produced in Mexico from cochineal. What is the source of that colour?
choices: A mineral found in volcanic rock
The bark of a tropical tree
note: Cochineal insects live on prickly pear cacti and produce an intense red. Indigenous producers developed ways to raise them, turning something tiny into a highly valued colour.

question: In a modern mariachi group, which brass instrument gives a bright sound above the guitars and violins?
note: Trumpets join strings and voices in the modern mariachi sound. The music carries local histories as well as celebrations, with a repertoire in Spanish and Indigenous languages.

question: Before Ritchie Valens made La Bamba a rock-and-roll hit, what was it?
choices: A traditional song from Mexico’s Veracruz region
note: Valens learned the song through his Mexican-American family and transformed it with electric guitar and a rock-and-roll beat. The hit carried an older Mexican dance song into a new musical world.

question: In Coco, a photograph on a family altar helps someone in the Land of the Dead return for a visit. What makes that possible in the film’s story?
choices: Someone among the living is remembering them
Their family has bought a special travel ticket
They have become a famous musician
They have been dead for exactly one year
note: Pixar gives remembrance a visible role: a photograph means someone is there to receive the visitor. The film turns an act familiar from Day of the Dead observances into a rule of its imagined world.

question: Mexican director Guillermo del Toro made Pinocchio with physical puppets. How did the filmmakers bring them to life on screen?
choices: Moving and photographing them a tiny step at a time
Filming marionettes moving continuously on strings
Drawing every frame over footage of live actors
Replacing every puppet with a computer-generated model
note: Physical puppets are moved in small steps and photographed to create the performance. The film returns a story about a wooden puppet to a world of objects that the filmmakers could handle.

question: For a Mexican lucha libre wrestler, which item can become an identity that continues into films and comic books?
note: The design helps turn the wrestler into a recognisable character. El Santo carried his masked identity beyond the ring into films and comics, becoming a figure in wider popular culture.

question: The cowboy is an icon of the American West. Which Mexican workers helped shape the skills behind that image?
choices: Silver miners carrying supplies by mule
note: Mexican vaqueros were part of the history that shaped cowboy work and culture. The familiar film image compresses a more varied world that also included Indigenous herders and Black cattle hands.

question: At Mexico’s 1986 football World Cup, what action by the crowd became famous around the world?
choices: Standing and sitting in sequence to send a wave around the stands
Jumping together while linking arms across each row
Turning their backs and bouncing after each goal
Raising coloured cards to build a giant national flag
note: The tournament helped give the “Mexican wave” a global audience. The crowd became part of the spectacle, creating motion around the stadium without anyone leaving their seat’s position.

question: In the Mexican dance often called the Hat Dance, a couple’s playful movements tell what kind of story?
choices: A family saying goodbye to a traveller
note: The jarabe tapatío uses the interaction between a pair of dancers to suggest flirtation. The broad hat and elaborate clothes frame a recognisable human story, even if you have never learned the steps.

question: Why did the football used at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico have such a striking black-and-white pattern?
choices: To stand out on black-and-white television
To help referees see which way it was spinning
To disguise the seams between the leather panels
To keep the ball cooler under the Mexican sun
note: The Telstar’s contrasting panels helped viewers follow the ball on television. That practical design became the football many people picture when they hear the word.

question: At the Mexico City Olympics, Dick Fosbury surprised viewers by clearing the high-jump bar in which way?
choices: He went over the bar backwards
He took off from both feet together
He carried a short pole for balance
He landed standing on his feet
note: Fosbury cleared the bar with his back facing it and landed on the mat. His 2.24-metre winning jump helped turn an unconventional technique into the familiar style of the event.
